A stone is projected horizontally at time t = 0 and falls. Air resistance is negligible. The stone has
a horizontal component of velocity vH and a vertical component of velocity vV.
Which graph shows how vH and vV vary with time t ?

hints: Notice the start at $t = 0$: the stone is projected horizontally, so $v_H$ starts at a non-zero value while $v_V$ starts at $0$.
With air resistance negligible there is no horizontal force but there is constant vertical acceleration $g$, so connect zero acceleration to constant $v_H$ and constant $g$ to $v_V = gt$.
Compare shapes: look for a flat non-zero line for $v_H$ together with a straight line through the origin for $v_V$.
walkthrough: At $t = 0$ the projection is horizontal, so initial $v_H$ is the launch speed and is greater than zero, while initial $v_V = 0$.
Horizontally there is no force when air resistance is negligible, so horizontal acceleration is zero and $v_H$ stays constant with time.
Vertically the only acceleration is $g$ downwards, so vertical velocity grows uniformly as $v_V = 0 + gt$.
On a velocity-time graph constant $v_H$ is a horizontal straight line above the $t$-axis, and $v_V = gt$ is a straight line of gradient $g$ starting at the origin.
Only the graph with a flat $v_H$ line and a straight $v_V$ line rising from $0$ shows both behaviours. This is option A.

A.explanation: $v_H$ is a non-zero horizontal line and $v_V$ is a straight line from zero, matching constant horizontal velocity and uniformly accelerated vertical fall.

B.explanation: Labels are swapped: the rising straight line from zero must be $v_V$, not $v_H$, because only the vertical motion accelerates.

C.explanation: $v_V$ cannot be a curve with increasing gradient because vertical acceleration is constant $g$, so $v_V = gt$ is a straight line.

D.explanation: $v_V$ cannot start at maximum and fall to zero; a horizontally projected stone starts with $v_V = 0$ and $v_V$ increases as it falls.
